seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: June, once Stevens Canyon Road is open and snow still covers the talus above Snow Lake and gives a long glissade down

May.reason: Stevens Canyon Road is usually still closed until late May, so the snow-covered approach means a long extra walk from the gate.

June.reason: Road open and snow still buries the boulder field and gully into the basin; firm morning crampon travel and a long glissade on the descent.

July.reason: Snow retreats from the gullies and a moat opens at the top of the snow below the summit block, which may need a hand line or careful climbing.

August.reason: Snow-free but a loose talus and scree slog above Snow Lake; the summit pitch is dry and the moat below the horn is at its widest.

September.reason: Stable, quiet conditions on dry rock and talus; shorter days and the lake is the last water, so start early.

October.reason: The first heavy snow closes Stevens Canyon Road, and fresh snow on the loose scree slopes makes the traverse to the summit horn slick.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: March to April, when the north face ice is fat and the Coleman Glacier crevasses are still well bridged

February.reason: The unplowed Glacier Creek Road adds miles of snow travel, short days squeeze a long approach, and storm slabs load the slopes above the Coleman Glacier.

March.reason: The north face ice is usually well formed and crevasse bridges are solid, but the approach often still starts miles down the snowbound road.

April.reason: Longer days and a shrinking snowline on the road, with the face's ice and mixed steps still frozen in; skis help on the approach and descent.

May.reason: Warming loosens the rock steps and ice, raising rockfall, and bridges on the Coleman Glacier soften; go only after a cold spell and start very early.

June.reason: The ice on the rock steps rots and sheds, rockfall increases, and large crevasses can open across the Coleman Glacier.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July to mid-September, after the basin snow and slab seeps are gone and before autumn rain wets the friction pitches

June.reason: Snow still fills the gullies in the basin, snow blocks can slide off the wall, Squire Creek runs high, and seepage wets the middle slab pitches.

July.reason: The basin melts out and the creek drops; early July can still have a seep on the crux slab section, which is dangerous friction when wet.

August.reason: Dry slab and the lowest creek; the south-facing granite bakes by midday, so climb the friction pitches early and carry plenty of water.

September.reason: Cooler air gives better friction on the Middle C slab pitches, the approach is at its easiest, and the rock is reliably dry between storms.

October.reason: Autumn rain arrives and the low-angle slab stays wet for days after; short days make the brushy approach and ford a headlamp affair.

March.reason: SR 20 is still closed across Washington Pass, so reaching the couloir means a long sled or ski trip from a winter gate into big avalanche terrain.

April.reason: If SR 20 has reopened, the couloir usually holds firm neve and solid WI4 ice; go after a cold, clear spell and be off the face before the sun hits.

May.reason: Right after a May reopening it can still be good, but by mid-May sun often bakes the ice to rotten slush and meltwater gouges deep runnels in the snow.

June.reason: The ice steps melt out or become too rotten to protect, and the sunny east-facing slopes release wet slides and rockfall into the couloir.

February.reason: The couloir and lower rock band are filled and frozen and the slide alder is leafless, but only go after a stable, settled snowpack.

July.reason: The route goes as a rock-and-snow climb, but the lower band is bare compact slab that is hard to protect and the approach brush is in full leaf.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: March to April, when the three couloirs are filled and the runnels hold ice, after the snowpack settles

January.reason: Rarely in shape: the runnels are often thin, the snowpack is unsettled, and the gated road adds miles in the dark.

February.reason: Couloirs can be filled and runnels iced after a freeze-thaw cycle; the gated road adds about four miles each way, and only go on a stable forecast.

March.reason: Longer days and a settling snowpack; freeze-thaw usually builds the best ice in the runnels, though conditions vary year to year.

April.reason: Classic month when snow is firm and bonded; start early, as warm afternoons bring rockfall and wet slides down the gullies.

May.reason: The runnels thin to rock and heat drives rockfall and wet slides; early-morning freezes and a fast pace are essential.

June.reason: Couloirs melt out to loose rock and the runnels are usually gone; rockfall is heavy on warm days.

June.reason: Crossings run high with runoff, especially the first and largest one, and snow patches can linger below the saddle and on the ridge.

July.reason: Creek crossings drop to rock-hops, the saddle and ridge melt out, and the meadows are in flower on this dry east-of-crest peak.

August.reason: Driest, lowest-water conditions for the creek fords; late-summer wildfire in the Teanaway can close the trail or fill the valley with smoke.

September.reason: Low creek and dry ridge rock with cooler days, but check for fire closures in the Cle Elum Ranger District, which can run into fall.

October.reason: Early snow can dust the loose upper ridge and summit block, and shorter days tighten a 9-10 mile, 3,800 ft outing.

November.reason: Snow covers the upper trail and ridge, cornices begin to form near the summit, and the wind on the half mile past the saddle is severe.

September.reason: Stable weather and cooler temperatures suit the burly roof and fingery cracks; late-month larch season brings heavy crowds to the Core.

October.reason: Short days make the 8-mile carry-over tight, and the first snows can coat Aasgard and ice the approach slabs.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July to early August, when snow still smooths the glacier and upper snowfield but the long approach through Conrad Meadows has melted out

June.reason: The long valley approach is usually open, but snow starts around 5,900 ft, stream crossings run high, and the glacier is still deeply snow-covered.

July.reason: Supportive snow over the Conrad and Meade glaciers and the summit snowfield, with the valley trail melted out; bugs are thick in the meadows.

August.reason: The glacier thins toward bare ice with open crevasses and more loose talus below the summit; start early for firmer snow.

September.reason: Cooler and bug-free, but expect bare ice, exposed crevasses and loose boulders; the upper snowfield is at its lowest angle.

October.reason: Early storms bury the approach and the glacier in fresh snow over bare ice, and the dirt road to Conrad Meadows can close with snow.
